utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to begin with Witness SA. First of all, we deem that psychiatric expertise should have been carried out, an examination first of all to see whether she really is a psychiatric patient and, secondly, whether she is able to testify despite of her illness because some persons can testify even though they are ill, and the fact that we are in the right is also shown by the Furundzija case where a witness who is a mental patient also testified and her testimony was accepted. She gave a statement, SA gave a statement on the 24th of April, on the 23rd of April, then there is also a record on the investigation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Counsel, would you please slow down. The translator has asked me to have you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Statement of the 18th of October 1994, C5; 24th of September, 1995, C6. The Defence thinks that the first three statements given directly after the events are the most accurate because her memory was the freshest at the time, and also there were no speculations at the time or conversations among the witnesses which might have influenced her testimony. In the first statements, SA stated that she did not recognise any of the attackers because they were masked and their faces were painted. Then, in contravention of Witness H's statement, Witness SA did not confirm that Witness H had told her that among the attackers, she had recognised Mirjan Kupreskic too. She said that she recognised only Zoran Kupreskic. In the first statement given to the police, she stated that she heard a call for all the people in the house to come out, and then when her husband came out, she heard a burst of gunfire. In her first statement, she said that she could not identify any of the soldiers, but she mentioned the people who were walking around the village and she named them. Among those she named were not -- neither Zoran nor Mirjan Kupreskic. On the 5th of May, SA gave a statement to HH who is now a court official. In this statement, she did not mention any of the perpetrators, but she used the term "soldiers." In her statement dated 5th of May, 1993, she talks about the fact that her elder daughter did recognise Zoran who was in the house allegedly with four other soldiers. In this statement, she also mentions Mirjan Kupreskic, but not as a person who was actually in her house but as a person she had seen before in the village wearing a uniform. If we compare her statement with the statement of Witness SA, then one can see that they differ in many points, and that is why we deem that the final testimony of Witness H cannot be used as a basis for making a factual determination. The stand taken by the Prosecution towards our clients is very interesting too because in their closing argument, the Prosecutor asked for 25 years in prison for them. And when they realised that the whole set of accusations against Witness KL is, in fact, exculpatory then they did not file an appeal against this, and they did have a very good reason not to lodge an appeal because everything that our clients said in their statements was either corroborated by witnesses or was corroborated later on by documents that emerged on a later date. Another interesting point when it comes to Witness H is that she even confused the colour of the uniforms worn by the persons who were in the house. When I talked about the fact that the villagers of Ahmici, or of the middle section of the village where the Kupreskic houses are located, in contravention to what is stated in the judgement that they did not in any way assist the attackers, that they did not provide them with any information and were not their guides, did not act as their guides, then in my appellant's brief, I mostly used the testimonies of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. However, of all the evidence that was accepted later -- all the evidence that was accepted later confirms their testimony. I'm referring to the testimony of one of the witnesses - you know the witness I mean - who specifically said that the group which set off from the Kupreskics' house contained also a person by the name of Mirjan Santic, who knew the terrain well because he was from the neighbouring village. Mirjan Santic died near the starting point. When we claimed that the villagers of Ahmici did not know that an attack was being prepared, we bore in mind the actual order of the events, and that is the fact that the decision to launch an attack was made at a meeting of the political leadership of the Vitez municipality, at Colonel Blaskic's place, on the 15th of April, in the afternoon of that day. And then a meeting was held with the military commanders and each of the commanders was given an order what the units under their command were to do. After that, the military police was transferred to the Bungalow and the attack was launched the way you know it was launched. When we talk about Zoran Kupreskic as a commander, then it is not enough to say that he was a commander or some kind of a commander, but we should also have a definition of what a commander actually is. According to the stand of the Defence counsel, a commander is a person who makes decisions and who entrusts the execution of their decision to a certain circle of persons; or a person who receives an order from the superior commander and relays it to his own subordinates with some elaboration, providing some details. If we take this definition of a commander as a starting point, then you can see that Zoran Kupreskic -- that as regards the attack on Ahmici, Zoran Kupreskic does not fit this definition, even if he were in a position in which he was on the 20th of the October, 1992, when he actually assigned guards to their duties. As regards Witness H, we should note that at the time she was 13 years old; she was, therefore, a child. Her testimony has not been corroborated by any other witnesses, and she was in a state of shock. As regards the fact whether or not the Kupreskic brothers were members of the HVO or not, I have already said that the Prosecution bases this on the document P353 [as interpreted], which we have challenged. I spoke about that very quickly yesterday, and now I will go over it in some detail since I do have some time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I warn you, you only have approximately three minutes more. Three minutes more. Three, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is important for us is the document that was issued at the time, and that's document P335. Attached to it is a list of persons mobilised in the period from the 16th to the 28th. Since the Kupreskic brothers are on this list as mobilised in this period of time, then it is impossible for them to be members of the army before the mobilisation, because if you are in the army, a member of the armed forces, you cannot join the armed forces again to be mobilised. And if you'd just allow me, I'd like to mention that P335 confirms that the attack was carried out by the military police, because the report, which is on pages 1 and 2 of this report, specifies that the mobile units carried out the first attack; and after the mobile units carried out the first attacks, the mobilised persons were brought to the front lines to hold the positions gained by the attackers or reached by the attackers. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think that I am in compliance with your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Radovic. All right, Ms. Glumac, you have, by my reckoning, till quarter past ten, till 10.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. First of all, I would like us to go into private session because I would like to say something that pertains to what my colleague Mr. Abell said last night, and I believe that this should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirjan Kupreskic was convicted for persecution as a crime against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute described in Count 1 of the indictment. The Trial Chamber in paragraph 779 of the judgement indicates that it had been confirmed that Mirjan Kupreskic was in action in Ahmici as an attacker on the 6th of April, 1993, and that he took an active part in those events. It is stated that he entered a house and that he evicted Sukrija Ahmic's house, Sukrija Ahmic from his house and his family. They used mostly the principle of mutatis mutandis. Everything that has been found as regards Zoran Kupreskic is also applied directly to his brother although I believe that there are some differences. So the question is: What evidence do we have to confirm the established -- the fact established by the Trial Chamber that Mirjan Kupreskic entered Sukrija Ahmic's house and expelled his family? As regards the material element of persecution that Mirjan Kupreskic committed, the Trial Chamber based itself on one single piece of evidence and that is the statement of Witness H. Witness H was used by the Trial Chamber to identify the perpetrators. She stated that when her family's house was attacked, that she hid in a shelter, and then her father left the shelter, opened the door, HVO soldiers killed him, and her family was expelled from the shelter. As she went out of the shelter she saw Zoran Kupreskic and then as she passed through the corridor, she saw Mirjan Kupreskic. The question is: How well could she have recognised or identified this person? Witness H said that the attack on her house took place between 5.20 and 5.30 in the morning, that there were no lights on in the house. As she passed through the corridor from the children's room, she saw a soldier on the staircase, and she recognised him as Mirjan Kupreskic. The witness, herself, says that the identification took just one second. She then turned her head away and went to the kitchen. She did not see him after that. When she saw him, she saw that he wore a black uniform and that his face was painted black. That he carried an automatic weapon, and hand-held rocket launcher slung on his back. What is the quality of the identification? First of all, it was just a glance. The witness testified that it was just a second. Secondly, it was very dark in the house. There were no lights on. We heard from other witnesses that that morning, in the village, it was dark. Witness K, who lived in a house next door, said that it was so dark that her husband was unable to find his trousers. Witness C used the phrase that it was "pitch dark." And other witnesses said that they had to turn on the lights in order to be able to see anything. It was a cloudy day. It was raining, and there was a fog, and there were no street lights because this was, after all, a village. Thirdly, the ability to identify someone was lessened because the face of the attacker was masked. It was painted black and the witness, herself, said that she was in a state of serious shock, that she was petrified a horror because her father had been killed and she was, together with her two sisters and her mother, was at the mercy of the attackers. If we take all this into account, it is doubtful whether the identification of that man standing on the staircase as Mirjan Kupreskic is accurate. There is a very real possibility that the witness may have made a mistake. Her conviction that she speaks the truth does not mean that she really did speak the truth. In this particular case, the quality of the identification was low because it was made after just a glance in very difficult conditions. The Trial Chamber did not admit any other evidence to the effect that Mirjan Kupreskic was indeed there in that place at that time that morning. In judgement, the Queen versus Turnbull quoted by the Trial Chamber and as I can see my learned colleagues are using it all the time, it is stated that when an identification is bad, if the identification was based on just a glance or a prolonged observation in difficult conditions, that in those circumstances, corroborating evidence must be found. In this case, there were no other pieces of evidence of this kind. The Trial Chamber bases its judgement only on the impression that Witness H made on it. The Trial Chamber states that the critical remarks on her testimony are weaker than the effect that she made -- the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. impression that she made on the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber says that the witness looked very confident and very convincing and that she had no doubt with respect to the identification that she carried out, paragraph 403. The fact that the witness seemed convincing does not mean that she said the truth. Even her conviction with regard to the accuracy of the identification does not mean that she said the truth. Professor William Wagenaar, who was an expert witness during the trial concerning problems of identification, he said that hundreds of research projects were carried out in order to distinguish between the conviction of witness in terms of whether he was speaking the truth and, on the other hand, the accuracy of the statement itself. This is exactly what he said [In English]: "... studies is that the relationship between certainty and correctness is very, very weak. There are many witnesses who are perfectly certain and they are wrong and there are many witnesses who are totally uncertain but they are right. The bottom line is that the amount of certainty expressed is much more an aspect of personality of that witness. Some are very certain witness. That's the way they are. Some other people are always uncertain even if they know the answer perfectly well. It's more an aspect of personality than an aspect of the quality of what they say or what they remember. So it is quite likely that an eye witness is totally sincere, totally honest, very convinced, does not assume that he or she can make a mistake, and still is very wrong about it." [Interpretation] Transcript 9862. That is to say that although the Trial Chamber was composed of three extremely competent and qualified Judges, if judgement is based on the impression that a witness makes, there is still the possibility of making a mistake. The witness was very convincing, and also she was convinced that she did not make a statement to an investigative judge before, that and she also said that the signature on the interrogation statement was not her own. She probably forgot that situation altogether. And having made such a statement again, she left the impression of a very convincing witness and a witness who was sincere and meant what she said. Also, the statement she made before the Trial Chamber differs considerably from the statement she made to the investigating judge. Most of these differences can be ascribed to the fact that time has gone by; however, some of them are very important, because, for example, if in one case she says that she saw the situation where the attackers killed her father and in the other situation she said that she did not see this, then the question is whether she spoke sincerely about everything she said. The Defence could challenge the credibility of this witness only on the basis of the differences between the statement she made before this Tribunal and the statement she made earlier on before the investigating judge, because the Defence did not have any other materials, because from Witness H no other statements had been taken. The only statement that the witness had was the statement that the witness gave in December 1993. It is precisely for that reason that the Defence proposed to the Court to call as a witness the mother of Witness H; namely, Witness SA, who was an eyewitness and who could give her account as to how the event actually happened. I shall just mention briefly that Witness SA - my colleague just mentioned this, but I had also put this in my brief because I thought that we'd missed this - she gave a different account than Witness H did. The difference was in the following: Witness SA claimed that the entire family, when they were in the shelter and when they heard soldiers in the house, decided to surrender and leave the shelter together; then the father was singled out and killed. Witness H said that her father walked out first on his own in order to surrender so that his family, all the people who were in the shelter, would have no further problems; and that is how she was in a position to talk to Zoran Kupreskic. In this first version of events that Witness SA gave, there was no such possibility at all; that is to say, the idea of the Defence to call a witness which had first been proposed as a Prosecution witness was based on the following: We wanted to find another statement made by Witness H and also another eyewitness of the events concerned. Since Judge Cassese, after having received a medical report on the poor health condition of Witness SA, decided that he would not subpoena her, and that the interests of the Defence were met through the fact that all the statements that this witness had made would be admitted into evidence, the Defence thought that in this way they were put in a position to discuss the statements that were included in the evidence; and that the substance of those statements could be confronted with the substance of Witness H's statements. The Defence did not think that these materials were being admitted in order to confirm that Witness SA, in her fifth statement, says that she recognised Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic among the attackers in the house. That would really be very, very bad, and it would be an ugly thing for the Defence to do. However, in the judgement, we realised that the only thing that the Trial Chamber took into account was precisely that, when Witness SA first mentioned Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic. And therefore I believe that the Defence had really been mistaken in its belief as to what the Trial Chamber would do. I'm mentioning, however, the statement made by Witness SA for a different reason here. She gave three statements after the events itself; two to the police and one to the State Commission for the Establishment of War Crimes, which had been founded by the Bosnia-Herzegovina government. These are witness statements C2 and C3. In the statement she gave seven days after the massacre in Ahmici, on the 23rd of April, 1993, Witness SA said that she did not recognise any one of the attackers because they were painted with different colours; however, Witness H recognised Zoran Kupreskic in the kitchen. Again, in the next written statement that she gave on the 9th of May, 1993, that is to say, less than a month after the event in Ahmici, she wrote that she did not recognise a single one of the masked soldiers; however, that her oldest daughter recognised a neighbour, Zoran Kupreskic, who was in her house together with four masked soldiers. In these statements, the witness did not mention that her daughter, in any situation, mentioned Mirjan Kupreskic as the perpetrator of the crime in their house, nor did she mention that her daughter ever mentioned Mirjan Kupreskic. Precisely the fact that Witness SA, on two occasions, said that her daughter had told her that her daughter had recognised Zoran Kupreskic but not Mirjan Kupreskic provides for the possibility to think that Witness H, only after a few months had elapsed, realised that actually the person whom she had seen on the stairs of the house was Mirjan Kupreskic, actually. I shall go back to Professor William Wagenaar again, who says during his testimony regarding the problem of identification, he says briefly that identification is not an ongoing process, that identification takes place very fast. Identification that is created later, so to speak, or that covers an extended period of time is no longer identification. If, after a certain amount of time elapses, we realise what we see, then this is not perception; then it is a question of reconstruction. Reconstruction is not perception, and it always takes place under the influence of information that a certain person receives over a certain period of time. Your Honour, could we just move into closed session for a short while. I will have to speak about Witness AT very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We can do that, Ms. Glumac. But may I ask you, can you consolidate your presentation so that anything that needs to be done in closed session could be done all at one time, maybe, rather than having to go out and in and out and in? In other words, we will go in now for your discourse on Witness AT. Will there be other instances in which you have to go into closed session? If so, it would be better to try to get them all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be another instance. However, I'm actually analysing only two pieces of evidence, so I would not like to confuse the two. I don't want to mix apples and pears. So I'll just ask for private session yet again very briefly; however, I don't want to violate the rules in any way. I do apologise, but I kindly ask for that to be done, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness KL, who charged Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic with multiple crimes, the commission of several killings in his house was -- his statement was not accepted by the Trial Chamber and the Kupreskics were acquitted as far as the commission of these crimes was concerned. The Trial Chamber concludes that the inconsistencies in his statement can be explained in the following way: That after talking to other persons, notably his granddaughter, Witness H, this witness convinced himself of what he had seen. This shows that the Trial Chamber does allow for the possibility of mutual influences between and among the members of a family and their thoughts concerning the possible perpetrators which is -- which resulted in certain evidence that was admitted during these proceedings. Witness H was barely 13 at the time when these events took place. It is a fact that the testimony of children is always taken with a bit of reservation because they attend -- they are susceptible to suggestions. If we take all these circumstances into account, first of all that the conditions for identification were very poor, that there is no supportive evidence. Then, in the area where this event took place, a military police unit had been sent, and then they had also received orders to that effect, the fact that the attackers were armed is exactly the way members of the military police had been armed, and also the fact that nobody mentioned Mirjan Kupreskic before December 1993 as a perpetrator of the crimes committed in Sukrija Ahmic's house. On the 17th of December, 1993 before an investigative judge, Witness H mentioned Mirjan Kupreskic for the very first time. According to her mother's statement, Witness SA's statement, that is, Witness H did not mention Mirjan Kupreskic before that. Three days after that, on the 20th of December, 1993, Mirjan Kupreskic was mentioned as a perpetrator of the crime by Witness SA as well. And then after that, in the beginning of 1994, Witness KL also mentions him. Neither Witness SA nor Witness KL who gave all of eight statements beforehand never mentioned Mirjan Kupreskic before that. When all these circumstances are taken into account and analysed, the Defence believes that there is reason to doubt whether Mirjan Kupreskic was really in Sukrija Ahmic's house that morning at all. That is, on the other hand, evidence upon which the judgement is based. In 421 and 789, paragraphs of the indictment -- of the judgement, it is said that Mirjan Kupreskic was an active member of the HVO. The Trial Chamber bases this conclusion only on the list of HVO members, and his activities on the 16th of April, 1993, that is to say, the testimony of Witness H. As for this list of HVO members, the Defence called many witnesses to show that this was not a credible document for a simple reason. This list was made in retrospect after the war was over, in June 1996, and in order to pay certain amounts of money or, rather, in order to obtain shares. This was a decision passed by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1996 that all participants in the war should be compensated in a certain manner for the time that they had spent in the war. Then both the Muslim and the Croat sides submitted lists that were considerably exaggerated, and all of this with the intention of obtaining more money for certain ethnic groups. On that list, there are some very old people, there are some children as well. According to law, the right to additional pay was exercised by all members of the active and reserve forces, members of the police force, members of the civilian defence, members of organisations that had defence tasks, participants in the war, disabled persons, families of war victims, et cetera. On the list there are also members of the village guards. Mirjan Kupreskic, in his Defence, said that he had been a member of the village guards during the period of one year. Mirjan Kupreskic did not sign that list; however, the Trial Chamber did not accept his statement. However, I would like to say that there is yet another list, and that is P371 which was submitted by the Prosecutor. This is a list that was compiled by the Defence office in Vitez. Again, the name of Mirjan Kupreskic is mentioned for the period from the beginning of 1992 until the 8th of April, 1992. That list was compiled at the same time in this same period, but that went all the way up to the 8th of April, 1992, that is to say, until the establishment of the HVO. This list clearly shows that Mirjan Kupreskic's name is on it, and next to his name is a note that he refused to sign this list. However, fundamental proof of the fact that information contained in the list of the HVO is incorrect is shown by Prosecutor's Exhibit P335 in which it says that in the period between the 16th of April, 1993 until the 28th of April, 1993, 486 persons were mobilised into the Viteska Brigade. In the text it says further on that most of the military conscripts mobilised from the day of the outbreak of the conflict onwards were directly taken to the first defence line. They are used in order to replace people who are already on the front line, after the first strike took place; that is to say, they are gradually brought in to replace soldiers from the regular forces. In this document, under number 109 is the name of Mirjan Kupreskic, which is to say that he had undeniably been mobilised in that period. If that previous list had been correct, then there would have been no reason to have him mobilised again, because that would have meant that he would have been an active member of the regular military forces. From that list we can see that it was a time of mobilisation, from the 16th of April, 1993 to the 28th of April, whereas Mirjan Kupreskic stated in his defence that the exact date of his mobilisation was the 18th of April, 1993, when the line at Pilica was established. According to the allegations derived from that list, he was mobilised into the Vitez Brigade. Even if he had been mobilised on the day of the outbreak of the conflict, on the 16th of April, then together with the Vitez Brigade he would have been located in the area of Veceriska and Vranjska, where the Vitez Brigade, according to the orders of Colonel Blaskic, was deployed. Apart from that, from the quoted text we can see that he would not have been involved in the first attack, but rather he would have been used later as a replacement on the first defence line. This piece of evidence shows that he, as a soldier of the HVO, could not have been present in Ahmici on the 16th of April. The Trial Chamber in the Kordic case established that the Vitez Brigade did not take part in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. In paragraph 703, the Trial Chamber says that there is firm evidence that Mario Cerkez, Commander of the Vitez Brigade, participated in attacks against Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Veceriska, and that there is no evidence that he bears any responsibility for the initial attack on Ahmici on the 16th of April, which was the responsibility of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police and not under his command. It also says that the brigade was not involved in the first attack, and any action in that area only happened after the massacre. If Mirjan Kupreskic had, in any way, joined in as a volunteer in the attack against Ahmici, then there would have been no need to mobilise him and he would not have been on the list of mobilised persons. I would only like to add that Mirjan Kupreskic was a civilian up to the day when he was mobilised. He had a regular job. This also brings a shadow of doubt on the evidence underlying the determination by the Trial Chamber that Mirjan Kupreskic was an HVO member. How much time do I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You have just under ten minutes left, till 10.15. No more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 430 of the judgement, it says that Mirjan Kupreskic participated in the attack against Ahmici as an HVO soldier, which is based on the testimony of Witness H. It also says that it is reasonable to conclude that his role and the role of Zoran Kupreskic were such that they were giving information known to the locals, and that their houses served as bases used by soldiers in the attack. The statement of Witness H has already been analysed and so has the fact that Mirjan Kupreskic was not mobilised on the 16th of April. As for reasonable conclusions regarding Mirjan Kupreskic's role in the provision of information and enabling soldiers to use the houses, we should say that such conclusions were not corroborated by any evidence. This allegation belongs to the area of speculation and guesswork, because not a single witness testified to such activity on their part. It is obvious that the basis for such reflections on the part of the Trial Chamber was the testimony of Witness H, who was believed by the Court. Can we go into private session for just a little while longer. I have only two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from that, if we analyse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just a moment until we get into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I interrupted a couple of times due to switching into private session. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, everybody gets interrupted and I think we have to have some kind of limits. Go ahead and complete your statement now within the next two minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thus, the statement contained in the judgement is inaccurate because the witness did not say that he had seen a group of soldiers in front of Zoran Kupreskic's house, but on the intersection between Zoran and Ivan Kupreskic's houses, in the afternoon, after 4.00 p.m. Also, from the testimony of a certain witness, it is evident that the military police had not received any orders to conduct any military reconnaissance. As for the decision on sentencing, I would only like to note that in paragraph 757 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber stated that with the possible exception of one of the accused, the main perpetrators were not tried here. We should also take into account the previous life and the lack of criminal record on the part of the accused and had there been no war, he probably would have been in no conflict with the law. Also in another place, the Trial Chamber states that it is a person of good character without ethnic or nationalistic prejudice or extremist standpoints. It is to be noted that he is his family circumstances should be taken into account, Mirjan Kupreskic is married and father to two children, two underaged children. One of his children has serious health problems due to the stressful war situation into which he had been born. He had a -- he has a complex picture of problems which makes him unable to attend school regularly. He was hospitalised. He has poor eyesight and he was determined to be mentally retarded. He has now been under observation at the centre for autistic children, and I think this can be a mitigating circumstance. All of this is corroborated by medical documentation which has been presented to the Appeals Chamber. Mirjan Kupreskic also supports his mother who is alone after the death of her husband, and due to old age and her difficult mental state due to the fact that both her sons are detained in The Hague suffers from serious chronic diseases of the thyroid gland, gallbladder and others, and heart disease and this, among others, is also a mitigating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Counsel is speaking very, very fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest with regard to sentencing that these circumstances be taken into account because I believe the pronounced sentence to be too high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me inquire whether any of my colleagues have questions for Ms. Glumac. No. All right. Thank you. Now, we will move on to Mr. Josipovic. Mr. Clegg, let me inform you, you do have an hour and 25 minutes. I do plan to take a break for the translators' purpose about 11.00 which would mean that your presentation would be roughly half over then. You can plan your organisation around that, and then you can complete it after the break, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly. May I just begin by indicating the topics that I hope to cover in the allotted time. I propose, initially, to return briefly to the standard to be applied to fresh evidence in the light of the Prosecution bundle of authorities that was served on me yesterday morning. Then to deal very briefly with the Prosecution appeal against conviction and sentence insofar as it impacts on Josipovic. Then to advance submissions in support of our appeal divided really into four parts. Part 1 is a submission that the Trial Chamber acted unreasonably in accepting the evidence of EE as a basis to convict. Secondly, an assessment of the impact of the additional evidence of AT. Third, consideration of the additional evidence of CA. And fourth, the question of sentence. Turning first, if I may, to the standard to be applied when fresh Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evidence has been admitted, I've now had an opportunity to read the bundle of authorities served by the Prosecutor yesterday, and I think I conceded in argument yesterday that the American authorities are divided, and it's a concession that I readily make. The first case in the bundle, the case of Huddelston clearly supports the Prosecution's contention that the appropriate standard is "would" and not "could." However, it supports the view that different standards can apply for different types of fresh evidence, and there's the Larrison test which is more akin to the test advanced on behalf of the appellants, and the Brady principle which has the more restrictive approach. This can be illustrated by reference to page 7 of the judgement in Huddleston where the more liberal lower standard described as the Larrison test, the Larrison test is not followed by the court there, and use words such as "probably would result in an acquittal," thereby support be the higher standard asserted by the Prosecution. The second American test of Joselyn, Billmyer, and Joselyn talks of the Brady principle in the headnote using the words, "... could reasonably taken to undermine the confidence in the district court's verdict." And again at page 7 in the judgement of the court there, the Brady principle is identified, and the two standards appear to divide upon a consideration of whether the absence of evidence at trial was due to a failure by the state to disclose material. We would respectfully invite the Court not to impose, as it were, two different standards in this Tribunal for the admission of fresh evidence which would bring a determination of where the fault lay for the absence of evidence at trial. The appellants here have, of course, established the due diligence test already before evidence can be admitted, and we would invite a rejection of the American two tier approach to the tests which appears, from my research, to be unique to the United States of America. The Australian cases that are quoted, I am fortified, support the proposition advanced by the appellant. The first is Gallagher which uses the test described as, "... a significant possibility that the jury, acting reasonably, would have acquitted the applicant of the charge if the new evidence had been before it." Those were words approved by the majority of the court, Chief Justice Gibbs, Justices Mason and Deane. Mr. Justice Brennan, in part, dissenting thought the, words "the likelihood of significant possibility," introduced a further nuance into the meaning that he did not like. Mr. Justice Dawson was with the majority, preferring the words, "A jury might reasonably acquit." Page 5 of the judgement puts that very firmly in the appellant's camp when the court says as follows: "However I would emphasise that no form of word should be regarded as an incantation that will resolve the difficulties in every case. No test can detract from the force of the fundamental principle. The appeal must be allowed if a miscarriage is showed to have occurred. It is only a practical guide to the application of that principle to say that the court will grant a new trial if having approached the matter with the caution that is always demanded when fresh evidence is produced in a criminal case having weighed the credibility for fresh evidence..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Clegg, when you are reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, I have a request for you to go just a bit slower from the translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Just picking it up, a line bag back, "... and having weighed the credibility of the fresh evidence and considered it's cogency in the light of the evidence given at trial, it considers that a jury might reasonably have reached a different verdict if the evidence had been available at the trial." And the final case, the Prosecution refer to is Mikelberg. Perhaps before I turn to that, I could just allude to the fact that the leading English case that's in the first book of authorities filed on behalf of Josipovic may be the House of Lords case of Stafford was cited and quoted in the judgement to the court in Gallagher in Australia with favour, with Mikelberg, the case that we've just looked at in Gallagher was applied and accepted, and the phrase that I quoted earlier of Mr. Justice Dawson, and I quote again, "A jury might reasonably entertain a reasonable doubt about the guilt of the appellant," and went on to use the word "significant possibility did not evolve a different standard." I'm in agreement with those statements. So assisted, as I'm sure the Court is, in relation to those authorities, certainly those from Australia support the view advanced by the applicant; those from the United States identify the dual test that I think is apparent in the papers and authorities lodged by the appellant Josipovic in his book of authorities. Can I just now turn for a moment to the Prosecution's appeal. I have conceded, in the light of the developing jurisprudence of this Court, and in particular the judgement of the Court in Jelisic, that the Trial Chamber was in error in acquitting Josipovic of the two counts that can perhaps best be described as those giving rise to cumulative convictions. The Prosecution have made it clear that they only want to reverse the acquittal. They are not inviting any sentence. There is no question of the matter being remitted to a Trial Chamber, as happened in the appeal of Tadic, for sentence to be reconsidered. But the Prosecution go on to say that the sentence on Count 1 was wrong, that it ought not to have been ten years and ought to have been 15 years. They say the Trial Chamber was in error in passing a lower sentence on Count 1. Now, for my part, it seems to me that this Appeal Chamber can make any observation obiter that it likes in relation to whether there is force in that submission or not, but the Appeal Chamber cannot increase the sentence on Count 1 even if it feels that the Prosecution submission is well-founded. The Rules of the Court set down a strict timetable for the parties to appeal a decision of a Trial Chamber, and each party must file notice of appeal within the time limits set out in the Rules. The Prosecutor has not appealed the sentence that was passed on Count 1, and indeed it wasn't until a year after verdict that they ever suggested that the Trial Chamber was wrong. If you look at their original brief filed in support of their appeal, there is no complaint about the sentence at all. Leave was then given, because of the developing jurisprudence of the Court, for them to file an amended brief, but there was no leave given to launch a new appeal upon which the time limits -- the time limits for which had long since expired. So insofar as the Prosecution is inviting the Court to reflect in an obiter statement that the distinction between the sentences passed on Count 1 and the other counts upon which Mr. Josipovic was convicted, I don't seek to address the Court one way or the other; but I do submit that insofar as they do appear to be suggesting - frankly, I'm not entirely sure if they are or not - that you should somehow intervene, and without either party actually appealing a sentence, of your own motion decide to increase it, I would submit that there is no power for you to do that under the Rules of the Court. You can only interfere with a judgement passed by a Trial Chamber if one of the parties to the proceedings appeals that decision, and neither party has appealed. So I don't propose to address the matter any further, but I do expressly invite clarification if I have misunderstood what the Prosecution say at the appropriate time so I can deal with it in the course of my response. Now, turning to the substantive appeal of Josipovic, the first ground of appeal is that the evidence of EE was so unreliable, so inconsistent that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have accepted that evidence and used it as the basis to convict. Now, I readily acknowledge that there is a very high standard for me to overcome in order to convince this Appeal Chamber that the Trial Chamber was wrong in accepting that evidence, and the test is high. I have to demonstrate that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have safely acted on that evidence. May I begin by looking at the judgement of the Trial Chamber and just remind the Court what the Trial Chamber held in relation to EE. At paragraph 503 in the judgement, and dealing with the findings of the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber held as follows: "Turning to the alleged direct participation of both accused in the conflict on the 16th of April, 1993" - and I pause, it's there referring to Josipovic and Santic - "the Prosecution relies on the evidence of the Witness EE who identified them both as participants in the attack on her house when her husband was murdered. Her evidence, together with the evidence called to cast doubt on it, have been analysed above. "The thrust of the criticism is that she has misidentified three other participants. It is accepted by the Trial Chamber that the witness was mistaken in her identification of Katava and Alilovic since there is compelling evidence that neither was in Ahmici that morning. It is not accepted that she was mistaken about Livancic since the only evidence concerning his whereabouts that morning came from two of his colleagues. However, it does not follow from the fact that the witness was mistaken in the identification of two of the participants that she was mistaken in the identification of the accused. "The witness struck the Trial Chamber as trustworthy and a careful witness who identified the two accused in a statement made three weeks after the offences and has not in any way retracted it. The Trial Chamber accepts her evidence and finds that Vladimir Santic and Drago Josipovic participated in the attack on the Puscul house. They were part of the group of soldiers who attacked and burned the house and murdered Muzafer Puscul." So that is the finding of the Trial Chamber, and there are two important matters to take into account. The first is that without the evidence of EE, all agree that there would be no case against Josipovic in relation to that count of murder. It is entirely dependent on her evidence. Take her evidence away, both sides agree there is no case. Now, I'm not going to read it because of pressure of time, but it's at paragraph 479 of the judgement that the evidence of EE is there summarised. Now, I don't shrink from suggesting that the Trial Chamber erred in accepting the evidence of EE, and whilst in no way seeking to analyse the words that the Trial Chamber used in that paragraph, 503, we have of course to remember that the burden and standard of proof being firmly on the Prosecutor, if it might be that EE's evidence is unreliable, then the verdict must have been not guilty. The evidence should have been rejected. Although the Trial Chamber does talk in terms of the burden appearing to be on the Defence when it says, "It is not accepted that she was mistaken about Livancic since the only evidence concerning his whereabouts that morning came from two of his colleagues." It is, of course, not incumbent on the Defence to prove that Livancic was not present; it is incumbent on the Prosecution to prove that he was. If I can just take the Court briefly to the evidence that we say was so inconsistent, so unreliable that no Trial Chamber, properly directing itself, ought to have convicted on that evidence. The relevant evidence begins at page 4082, when the witness was asked these questions: "Who did you recognise standing there at that time?" This is outside her house, just before her husband is killed. It's when the soldiers come, take him away, take him round the corner and he is shot. Answer: "Vlado Santic, Zeljko Livancic" - more about him later because he's somebody that features in the evidence of AT - "Drago Josipovic, Marinko Katava, Karlo Cerkez." Now, in that answer, the inclusion of the person Marinko Katava is highly relevant. That person could not be there. Compelling evidence proved that person was miles away in Vitez, and that was accepted by the Trial Chamber in that passage of their judgement we've just looked at. So right at this crucial part of the witness's evidence, she is saying that Marinko Katava was present at the time when her husband was killed, when we know that person cannot be there, on the finding of the Trial Chamber, in the face of compelling evidence. The questioning continued confirming the presence of that person who we know was not there. "At that time did you recognise anyone else in these two seconds?" "At this moment I just cannot think. I know Katava was there," well, he wasn't, "Cerkez was there, Zeljo, Santic, Josipovic." Then a little later, at page 4087, she dealt with the person Stipo Alilovic, who has the nickname Brko. She said this: "... there was only one HVO soldier standing here," that's at her house, "just one, and he looked at me like this," and demonstrated to the Court. "This was Stipo Alilovic, nicknamed Brko." "How long did you look at this Stipo Alilovic at that moment?" "Just for several seconds. It was a matter of seconds. It wasn't slow motion. Everything occurred in a matter of seconds. Everything they did, this whole operation." "What did you recall seeing or hearing next?" "Perhaps a second or two or three, it's very hard for me to tell the time, in one split second again, a group of soldiers appeared. Stipo Alilovic stood leaning against this wall at this first step. Zeljo Livancic stood next to him. After him was Drago Josipovic and Karlo Cerkez at this point." Then I just skip three lines. "This Brko, Halilovic Stipo, held a bomb, a grenade in his hand. Next to him was Zeljo." And then skipping three lines, "Stipo Alilovic came up and said, 'What do I do with the grenade?' he says to Zeljo. Zeljo looked at us, looked at me, looked at my children. I'm sorry, I apologise for using this word. He says, 'Out, get lost.'" Now, all agreed or, at any rate, probably I am true to say all agreed that the finding of the Trial Chamber was against compelling evidence that Stipo Alilovic was in Holland on the day of the Ahmici massacre and that was a finding of fact that the Trial Chamber made and yet this Witness EE who gives the only evidence against Josipovic on the count of murder has him standing next to her holding a bomb. And, indeed, the examination-in-chief of prosecuting counsel at trial reflects in those questions a desire for the witness, if possible, to retreat from her identification of this witness by emphasising how many seconds she had and so on. Because the Prosecutor at trial knew that the evidence that the witness was in Holland not only existed but was compelling. And indeed, so significant was this evidence that in the closing brief of the trial submitted before the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, in an attempt to circumvent the embarrassment this evidence caused them tried to suggest that it's possible that without anybody knowing, and without his passport being stamped, Stipo Alilovic may have somehow spirited himself back to Bosnia for the day in order to turn up with the grenade and then get back again. That is contained in the Prosecution closing brief as a sensible possibility in order to overcome this evidence. Well, the Trial Chamber rejected that, and they came to the conclusion that there was no doubt that Stipo Alilovic, just like the last witness, was not there. So you have a picture whereby the crucial witness, the only witness who gives evidence against Drago Josipovic in relation to this count of murder has wrongly identified two people who can be proved to be elsewhere by evidence that is, as the Trial Chamber said, compelling. There is at least a question mark over a third whom the Trial Chamber was not prepared to accept was elsewhere as the only evidence came from two witnesses. It's a very far cry from being sure that he was there. The evidence of the witness was reinforced just a couple of pages on, 4089 she records this conversation with a man who was in Holland, "Then Stipo Alilovic asked what I already told you about, what he'd do with the Han grenade. Zeljo looked at me and the children," and she repeats the evidence that she gave earlier. And then she said that her husband was then taken away by the two men and shot. I can give you the reference for the Prosecution's closing speech where they put forward the -- one might say slightly desperate suggestion that this witness had somehow got an away day ticket to get back to Bosnia for the massacre, it's day 112 on the 11th of September, 1999, page 96, line 13. It's a demonstration of how important the Prosecutor thought this evidence was. Later at page 4153, the witness confirmed again, Marinko Katava was present. We know for sure that's wrong. And then a moment or two later, she says this, "Stipo Alilovic, Stipo was there too, sir. Stipo Alilovic nicknamed Brko. He has a dark complexion and he has a beard and he has a moustache." "So he's characteristic, you would say he's..." "Yes," said the answer "he has dark hair, he has a moustache, he has a beard, he has a dark complexion." "You said you saw him a little later on, but it doesn't matter, you now say you saw him in that instance?" "Yes, I saw him then ..." And then on the next page, 4155, she says, "So you saw them all, Livancic, Santic, Brko, Alilovic, Stipo Alilovic, nicknamed Brko, Katava, and all of them?" "Yes, I saw all their faces." "Madam," said the questioner, "this incident is undoubtedly something you will remember for your entire life, the trauma you have experienced." "Thank you for understanding." Probably fair to observe that the person cross-examining was actually getting her to reinforce what he knew to be a totally and utterly false identification. 4164: Stipo Alilovic, the man in Holland, "Stipo Alilovic ordered Zeljo Livancic to take my husband Muzafer, and he took him behind the shed. Immediately afterwards I heard a burst of gunfire. After that, I never saw my husband again." That was a quotation put to her from her earlier statement. She accepted that she made it. The Trial Chamber accepted she made it. That man who took her husband away and shot him was in Holland. There's a debate about Alilovic ordering it. Then there's more about the description of Alilovic, the cap he was wearing on page 4170, "... he a quite a few bandoleers with bullets on it, and the kind you fill a rifle with at the same time as you shoot." And then 4174, a description of Katava, all agree wasn't there, couldn't be there in Vitez. "Katava didn't a have a cap and Cerkez didn't have a cap, but Alilovic had a cap too." Then she says Katava played a part in taking the husband behind the shed. 4187, "The people you saw on the terrace and recognised, Zeljo Livancic, Stipo Alilovic, nicknamed Brko, Marinko Katava, Vlado Santic. You explained to the Court that you know these individuals very well." "Yes, certainly, of course." All agree that this witness knew these two witnesses very well. The person who was, in fact, in Holland and the person who was, in fact, in Vitez. 4188, I won't read the descriptions that are gone into in great detail but it ends with there, "... and therefore are you quite sure that Stipo Alilovic was there?" "Yes, I'm 100 per cent certain." The next page, Marinko Katava all know wasn't there. "So you were able to see him, that's Marinko Katava, very well as well?" "Yes, that's correct, sir." "Where do you know Marinko Katava from?" "I know Katava very well, Marinko." "Yes, and I'm asking you, where do you know him from?" " Well, Marinko, I know that he worked in the Impregnacija company. His wife is a pharmaceutical worker, and his father is an eye doctor, and when I wanted to get my licence, I went to glasses I went to see them." And then, "... everything you said about Marinko Katava leaves no doubt that Marinko Katava would be at your door." "I am completely certain that he was there." First answer on page 4190. And then slightly repetitiously, 194, 100 per cent certain, again, in relation to Stipo Alilovic. So I don't shrink from submitting to this Appeal Chamber that in the light of that evidence, the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that the evidence of Witness EE was a safe basis to convict anybody. The slightly curious finding of the Trial Chamber was that the witness was mistaken about the identification of those two individuals. Accepting that at face value, if a person can be mistaken about somebody they know very well indeed standing in front of them holding a bomb, and somebody they know very well indeed taking their husband around the corner and shooting him dead, then the quality of that witness's perhaps is only a reflection of the trauma they suffered that day is frankly shattered, and it cannot be a safe basis upon which to convict Drago Josipovic or anyone else. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There is here no doubt the Trial Chamber have found conclusively that those two individuals were not there, and the evidence independently proved it conclusively. And in the face of that, we don't shrink from saying that we have satisfied the high test that the Rules of this Tribunal place upon me, when appearing in an appellant capacity, to satisfy this Chamber that no reasonable tribunal could conclude that that evidence was a reliable and safe basis upon which to convict. At its height, one could say that it might be true, but I ask the question rhetorically: Having seen those transcripts, can anyone say that her evidence must be true in relation to Josipovic or to use the words, "Can you be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that having made a fundamental error in relation to two people she knew well, why on earth should she be right in relates to a third?" And the only distinction being that unlike the other two, Drago Josipovic was in the village that day, but that only establishes it as a possible candidate for being there. It doesn't help prove that he was there. All it means is that he's unable to prove, with the compelling evidence that was available to Katava and Alilovic, that he could not have been there because he was either in Holland or in Vitez. I say, will turn later to what the additional evidence demonstrates. There is very real doubt about the presence of Josipovic which the Trial Chamber did not conclude was there, only concluded that the Defence had not proved was not there. That's rather turning the burden of proof on its head. We say that so far as the evidence of EE is concerned, it was rejected rightly in relation to Josipovic. It was rejected rightly in relation to Katava and, as a consequence, it cannot be used as the safe basis upon which to convict. It is dangerous evidence. Evidence from which a miscarriage of justice has traditionally, in the history of criminal courts, been known to flow from. There is really nothing more dangerous than an identifying witness who can be demonstrated to make mistake after vital mistake in pointing out who is present. That is what we have here in this case, and I repeat, I make no apology for it, without EE, there's no case on this murder count, and it is an unsafe basis upon which to convict. It also has an impact on the conviction on Count 1, but I accept it is not the only evidence on Count 1. But if you look at paragraph 810 of the Trial Chamber judgement, you will see how it is incorporated into the evidence in Count 1 and one, perhaps, cannot say without it what conclusion the Court would have come to in relation to that count. I think I may have had -- may have a wrong reference. 810, sorry. It's 810 where the Trial Chamber incorporates the evidence of EE into the basis of conviction on Count 1. Now, so far as the resolution of the appeal is concerned, if my submissions are well-founded in relation to EE, then it is not a case for a retrial. This is a case where I have satisfied the Appeal Chamber that no Trial Chamber, properly directed, could accept that evidence and therefore the convictions should be quashed. And that is what we submit is the only proper outcome when this evidence is analysed. I see the time is just coming up to 11.00. I'm now going to move to an assessment of AT.

utterances.text: I think this is a good time then to take our break until 11.30 and then you'll have another I think it's 40 -- yeah, 40 minutes, I think, to complete your presentation. So we are adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, you can resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I now turn to the additional evidence of AT. The first matter to resolve is the proper ambit of the Appeal Chamber's ruling on admissibility, dated the 29th of May of this year. We have proceeded upon the basis that the Appeal Chamber admitted the evidence of AT, under Rule 115, in the case of Vlatko Kupreskic, and therefore, as the Appeal Chamber said in paragraph 17 of their decision, "the other parties are entitled to avail themselves of it." Those words, we submit, are perfectly clear, and we have proceeded upon the basis that we who represent Drago Josipovic are entitled to avail ourselves of the evidence of AT that has now been admitted before this Appeal Chamber. The Prosecution take a different view. They have submitted that your decision ought to be viewed restrictively, and that the decision in relation to the application on behalf of Drago Josipovic, which is in paragraph 9 of your decision, namely, that the requirement of credibility was not made out and therefore AT's evidence was not reasonably capable of belief, fail to satisfy the test of 115 so far as Josipovic is concerned. The stance of the Prosecutor is, to some extent, a late stance, because following the decision, we applied to the President of the Tribunal for access to the closing brief in the Kordic case that was filed confidentially by the Prosecution in that case, obviously because it could impact on the assessment of the evidence of AT in this appeal. In responding to that application, the Prosecution did not invite the interpretation of the decision that they are now putting forward somewhat late in the day, but indeed conceded that relevant parts of the Kordic closing brief could be revealed to the Defence, as it has been, presumably for incorporation in my submissions before you today. So we have a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Clegg. Do you have to go into private session for any of your discussion of AT testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I will do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: -- but I think I'm all right at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The first matter to be resolved is whether the words contained in paragraph 17 of the decision do entitle the Defence to rely upon the evidence of AT in this appeal. What the Appeal Chamber ruled was that other parties are entitled to avail themselves of it. The word "other" must embrace parties that are not included in the application that was then being considered in that paragraph and must embrace Drago Josipovic. Such an approach would be consistent, we submit, with common sense. Because if the evidence is to be admitted before the Appeal Chamber, as it has been in the appeal of Vlatko Kupreskic, then it is really absurd that, in considering an appeal, the Appeal Chamber would be entitled to hear from the Prosecutor as to the evidence of AT and its impact - because it's admissible inter partes between them and Vlatko Kupreskic - but that I wouldn't be able to say anything about it on behalf of Drago Josipovic, even though the very evidence that is relevant is being spoken about by other parties to the appeal. The position is similar to what one might have before a Trial Chamber. One could envisage a situation where evidence could be ruled inadmissible insofar as one defendant was concerned - and he would not be allowed to call that evidence because it wasn't relevant to any matter so far as his trial was concerned - but it could be relevant in relation to a second defendant. If admitted before the Trial Chamber, it becomes evidence in the trial and all parties may comment on it. All parties would be entitled to ask the witness questions, and all parties could seek to adopt what the witness said in the course of their closing submissions. So we submit that the door is already open as a consequence of the Appellate Chamber ruling on the 24th of May as expressed in paragraph 17, in fact, I think it's the 29th of May. I correct myself. As specified in paragraph 17 where it says that other parties are entitled to avail themselves of it, "it" being the evidence of AT. The matter was first raised by the appellant in his supplemental appellant's brief filed on the 14th of June at paragraph 211 and also dealt with in the brief of argument filed under Rule 113 on the 18th of July at paragraph 4(1) going through to 4(5). The alternate submission that I advance with due diffidence before Appeal Chamber is that the decision made on the 29th of May was insofar as the decision concluded that the evidence of AT was not reasonably capable of belief was decided per incuriam and, upon reflection, is a decision which cannot be sustained and that the Appeal Chamber, of course, has the power to remedy any decision that it has made in error in the past. The decision that the evidence was not capable of belief was not made against a background of the Appeal Chamber being apprised of the detail of the evidence of EE that I have taken the Appeal Chamber through today demonstrating how the witness was acknowledged to be wrong in relation to two witnesses she had asserted 100 per cent certainty about when identifying at the scene. Secondly, the Appeal Chamber did not know, because it had not been disclosed, that in the -- and I just pause, I think we ought now to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The evidence of CA has been admitted by the Appeal Chamber, and the witness speaks of a relevant telephone call from DD. The Prosecution has served a statement from DD of which we acknowledge and is relevant and, in fairness, ought to be admitted before a Appeal Chamber, and that evidence is to the effect that no such telephone call was made. The importance of the telephone call is really twofold. Firstly, it may, depending on its contents, cast doubt upon whether DD few the fate of her husband and son in the aftermath of the massacre in Ahmici. And now, more significantly, the fresh statement served by the Prosecutor has identified a lie by a witness called at trial. Either CA is lying and DD phoned her, or DD is lying when she says she didn't. There is no way that the Appeal Chamber can resolve that issue because you haven't heard the witnesses, and one of them must be lying. If DD is lying, then it must affect her credit. Her credit would be highly material to the acceptance of her evidence by the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber knew that she was lying about that phone call, it may well cast doubt on the remainder of her evidence. It might be that in the light of that evidence, they would have resolved their conclusion as to her in a different way. Finally, and very briefly, there is an appeal against sentence. We do submit that the sentence of 15 years is excessive in all the circumstances in this case bearing in mind particularly the role and standing of Josipovic as found by the Trial Chamber, his voluntary surrender to this Tribunal, and the assistance and help he gave on the evidence to Muslim families, particularly that of CA, on the day of the massacre himself. Unless I can assist the Chamber any further, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. Any questions? Okay. Thank you. We will now begin with the presentation of Mr. Santic on appeal. You'll have 45 minutes, 45 minutes or however it comes out afterwards. So we'll go ahead and have you begin until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, perhaps it would be useful for better understanding of the Defence of Vladimir Santic to remind ourselves of certain facts because it turned out in the Prosecutor's brief that certain things need Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to be clarified. The first thing we want to emphasise is the position of the appellant after he withdrew parts of his appeal on the 25th of October, year 2000. Of course a certain doubt could have appeared as to what arguments made in the appeal remain relevant, and in our submission of the 12th of June, year 2000, the Defence supplemented our appeal which I believe now presents a clearer picture of our arguments. However, it is a fact that the Prosecutor still remains doubtful as to what remains current in the position of the Defence, and I must specify that it is only section 3 of our appeal. It is relevant though, and I will elaborate it, namely the claims made in paragraph 1.2 which is the relationship between the accused and the Jokers, and the appellant will try to clarify this link. Also relevant remains what is stated in item 2 of the appeal and here, I agree with the Prosecutor that also relevant remains the content of item 3. Now that we have clarified what remains to be discussed and what arguments are still relevant after the withdrawal of part of the appeal on the 25th of October, year 2000, I will now proceed in the sequence that I have explained. Your Honours, I will beg for your understanding when I ask for us to go into closed session in parts of my address perhaps more so than others have done today. I will avoid repetition in comparison to what my learned colleague Mr. Clegg has said, because he really exhaustively analysed pieces of evidence, and since my client and his client played the same role, according to the indictment, I will, as I said, avoid repetition. In paragraph 827 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber determines it is brief so I will quote it: "The accused played the role of the commander of the military police unit and the commander of the Jokers and in that capacity, he passed on the orders of his superiors to his men and besides that, his presence on the scene of the attack is seen as an additional encouragement." In the understanding of the Defence, as we have stated in our appeal, these conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber based on the derived evidence made -- presented by the Prosecution is wrong. Here in our appeal in item 1.1, we elaborated in detail where the error lies and I will not go back to this part. The central issue of this entire position of the defendant is the following: Was he, indeed, as determined by the Trial Chamber, the commander of the attacking forces in Ahmici, and it is doubtless that the attack took place by the military police. So it is essential to look at the basis for this determination by the Trial Chamber. It is important to note that there is no piece of evidence or testimony to corroborate this allegation of the Prosecutor. What do the witnesses called by the Prosecution and accepted by the Trial Chamber actually say as to the fact that the defendant Santic was the commander of the military police units in the attack against Ahmici? All the witnesses that have been heard actually speak about their acquaintance with the defendant, that is, the accused. They also speak about his formal status. But before the events and after the events, as far as the relevant period is concerned, that is the 16th of April, 1993, and the role of the accused as seen by the Trial Chamber, these witnesses do not say a word. Nobody speaks about his status in the relevant -- at the relevant time, that is the 16th of April, not even the witness whose statement was commented upon by my colleague and whose testimony is of very contestable value. Even she does not identify the -- even though she does identify the accused, she does not speak about his status. We can see from the judgement that the Trial Chamber paid special attention to the testimony of Witness AA, and there are several references to this testimony in paragraphs 88, 134, and 447. This witness, I should like to remind you, only confirmed the accused was a member of the military police. However, what is very important to stress here is that this witness, or so it seems from the judgement made by the Trial Chamber, was very important but he left the area in question in April 1993. So it is difficult to conclude from this testimony what the role of the accused was in the relevant time, that is, the 16th of April. That he left the area in April 1993 is evident from paragraphs 3 of the judgement -- excuse me, from the transcript page 3775, pages 18, 19. So the conclusion is absolutely wrong; however, this could be assumed, this could be an assumption made on the basis of the position of the accused before and after the events, but it could not be firmly established what his position was at that given moment, let alone the fact that this testimony of Witness AA, judging by the interpretation given to that testimony in the judgement, its authenticity is also questionable, and we have explained this in our appeal. What was the real status of the accused on the 16th of April, 1993, which is the only thing relevant? Not the witnesses Sulejman Kavazovic or Zaim Kablar, neither of these witnesses could say anything about this. Both of them speak about events before or after the relevant time. One of these witnesses confused the accused with another person, and we have Exhibit D5/6 which demonstrates that this witness is not reliable, because he spoke about a completely different person who bears the same name as the accused. Another witness who speaks to the link between the accused and the Jokers, as established in the judgement, actually says the contrary. He says that at that time the unit was commanded by Pasko Ljubicic and not the accused Vladimir Santic. The judgement also proceeds from certain statements which were found by an expert heard during the proceedings, and that is military expert Dzambasovic - and we have no objection to that - but he spoke about the assumed position of the accused. This witness did not speak to the actual events. This witness was to clarify certain military issues and explain a certain military doctrine, and thus this witness can by no means confirm the allegations of the Prosecution, cannot be used for that purpose, and his testimony cannot be used as a basis for the conclusions made by the Trial Chamber. I will also speak about another witness and Prosecution Exhibit 390. From the statements and testimonies of all the witnesses I have mentioned so far, it cannot be concluded beyond any reasonable doubt, as was done by the Trial Chamber, that the accused had the actual status of commander of the units that carried out the attack in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, and not a single witness who made the identification speaks about the status. Out of all the witnesses who have been heard with regard to this circumstance said that the accused seemed to have a commanding position. And I should like to remind you here of Exhibit D16, which doubtlessly demonstrates that the commander at the time was Pasko Ljubicic. It is not the only exhibit. There are many other exhibits which clearly show who was the commander at the time. With all due respect, Your Honours, I would also like to draw your attention to the judgement rendered by this Tribunal, IT-95-17/1-T, which determines that the commander of the Jokers, so in contravention to the conclusion reached by this Trial Chamber, was Anto Furundzija. In the very same judgement, this circumstance that he was the commander is taken as an aggravating circumstance for the sentencing. We also had the testimony of Witness GG who confirmed that the commander of the Jokers was Ante Furundzija. When it comes to the order that the Trial Chamber discusses, concluding that the accused issued orders in his capacity of a commanding officer to his subordinates, no such order has been presented before this Court. And then we have a real reason to ask: What was the basis on which the Trial Chamber based its conclusions? There are no orders issued by Santic regarding the attack on Ahmici. If we deal very briefly with this issue, and we have to do this just to go to what has been said in the Kordic judgement, in paragraph 610, it is stated that after a political decision had been made -- perhaps I could just very briefly ask you to go into private session, just for a very short time, to deal with this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, when I claim that there is no evidence, that no evidence has been adduced before the Trial Chamber as to any orders that the accused Vladimir Santic may have issued, in light of the claims by the Prosecution and the conclusions which I deem to be wrong drawn by the Trial Chamber, I have to stress that it is quite understandable. And if we -- when we go on to look at the testimony by Witness AT, it is quite clear that these orders do not exist. They could not have been produced before the Court because the accused could not have issued any such orders because he was not in the role of a person who would be entitled to issue such orders. I have to remind you that certain orders were produced before the Trial Chamber, and they were registered as Defence Exhibits D36/2, D37/2, and D38/2. Witness CE [as interpreted] was heard before the Trial Chamber and he explained the nature of these orders.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: It is Witness CI.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But these orders have nothing to do with this accused and these orders do not relate to him. So when we take all this that I have just spoken about into account, and this is the only thing that has been -- the only things that have been presented to the Trial Chamber, then we are entitled to ask ourselves the following question: whether, on the basis of these witness statements, one can draw a reasonable conclusion that the accused was, indeed, the commander of the military police in the action in Ahmici; and whether the accused was the commander of the Jokers units, which is mentioned quite often. There is no other evidence. I have presented them very briefly. Some of this has been presented in our appellant's brief, and this oral argument is merely a supplement to what has been written out in our appeal. The conclusion, then, is that the Trial Chamber reached wrong conclusions, and that nobody would be able to determine beyond reasonable doubt on the basis of this evidence that Vladimir Santic had a commanding role, the role of the commander of all the forces taking part in the attack on Ahmici village. Of course, the Defence wishes to clarify the actual role played by Vladimir Santic in these events. To this end, we will be referring to the testimony of Witness AT, and I would now like to ask for your indulgence once again, I would like to go into private session as is usually the case when we discuss testimony by Witness AT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [No translation]
