utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The Defence wishes to reiterate, to repeat what has been said. So this is an aspect of the same problem of the status of the accused, his commanding role as it has been established by the Trial Chamber. In section 2 of the appeal, the Defence has stated that the Appeals Chamber has made a mistake when assessing his commanding role when he was not notified that his alleged status will be used as aggravating circumstance. So he was not able to contest these facts during the trial. We're not talking about any errors on the part of the Defence counsel which would be outside of the limits of the due diligence. This is a completely different issue because there is nothing in the indictment up until that time that would indicate that the accused Santic would be treated as a commander. Quite the contrary. All the allegations against him and the others were based on his personal responsibly, individual responsibility defined in Article 7(1) of the Statute. But before the end of the proceedings but after the presentation of the evidence, in his final brief, the Prosecutor indicated that his status as the commander will be relevant, then up until then, the Defence did not adduce any evidence relating to the status of the commander for one very simple reason, because it was not relevant. So only after the end of the presentation of evidence, the Prosecution stressed this and stressed that the role of the accused, that the responsibility of the accused is much more serious because he had a commanding role. This was the first notification that was received and it was received only after the end of the presentation of evidence. When this notification was received, it was too late for the accused to present any evidence that might cast some doubts on the allegations. Since he had not been notified in a fair manner and since he had not been given an opportunity to defend himself against these allegations that he was in the command, the Defence deems that the sentencing was in contravention of Article 21 (4)(a) of the Statute. We would like to remind you of the fact that in the indictment which attached as Annex A to the judgement treated the accused -- or rather does not treat the accused as a person with a higher degree of culpability. It merely states that he was an HVO soldier in Vitez. This is a quote that he was an HVO soldier in Vitez. I'm quoting from the indictment. In sections 2 and 3 of the appeal, the Defence presented, in corroboration of these claims, regarding the prompt notification and the affording the opportunity to adduce evidence to refute the allegations. We presented many views that are contained in the judgement. I will not repeat them now. I would just like to refer you to section 2.3 of my appeal. Now, I would like to merely stress that all the views contained in the judgement and in our -- also I would like to refer to many national legislations, all these instruments indicate that the accused should have been told about this. He should have been informed in order to afford him the opportunity to defend himself against this. I would like to remind you that the international covenant on human and political rights and the Statute of the International Court used the same language, both instruments used the same language guaranteeing the right to the accused, let me quote, "That he will be informed quickly, promptly and fairly in the language he understands about the nature of the accusations against him." The nature of the accusations includes all the relevant factors and facts and, of course, all those factors which are relevant for the sentencing. And it is precisely in the sentence that had been imposed on the accused that the weight of the commanding role is stressed. But because he was not given the opportunity to defend himself, the sentence imposed on him was capricious and unfair. Therefore, the evidence that he was or was not a commanding officer is relevant for any part of the trial because it was only obtained after the trial. In the absence of the notification that a heavier sentence would be imposed if he were established to have been a commander, it was not impossible to defend himself against him, and he only became aware of that was in the final brief of the Prosecution when the Prosecution requested a higher sentence to be imposed because of his commanding role. There is nothing wrong with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as they stand now, but it is possible that the situation as it existed up until 1998 led to these errors. That was a time when it was decided that any evidence pertaining to the sentence were to be adduced later. To illustrate these claims and to illustrate how important it is to notify, to inform the accused that he would be treated in this manner, I will use the following story or the following metaphor: The accused was like a pilot flying blind without any navigational equipment, any charts. He was unable to prepare himself because he did not have the appropriate information. It would have been easy for the Prosecution to inform the Defence that they would be seeking a heavier penalty because of the commanding role of the accused, and if it would have been done in the course of the presentation of the case, both sides would have been able to address the issue and the Trial Chamber -- and the Appeals Chamber would now have to decide this issue once and for all. Your Honours, if I'm right, I still have five minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in this section of my presentation since. In my second part, I would like to address a whole new issue that has to do with sentencing. With your permission, it is now, of course, up to your judgement whether we should have a break now and then if, perhaps, I could continue presenting our views on the sentencing after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused Vladimir Santic has had a strict sentence imposed on him. It is too strict and unfair. The accused Santic has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for the crime of persecution. That sentence is two times longer than any sentence imposed on anyone in this group. It is double the sentence that was passed with respect to the accused Josipovic for persecution. What are the reasons for imposing such a strict, unfair sentence? That was explained by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 862 in the judgement. It is not very long, Your Honours, so by your leave I'm going to read that part of the text. However, I wish to draw your attention to the following as well: From now on, I shall be drawing your attention to circumstances that were of decisive importance in sentencing. I wish to show that the Trial Chamber made a mistake in respect of this sentence. Then there's also yet another group of circumstances that we discussed here in this court. The Defence provided some evidence; however, no mention was made of this in the judgement, and the Defence believes that this is of relevance in terms of adequate sentencing. Finally, I shall speak of those circumstances which, by the very nature of things, when the judgement was passed, were not mentioned at all and were yet important. Had this been known at the time, in the opinion of the Defence, this certainly would have contributed to a proper decision on sentencing. The Trial Chamber believed that on the 16th of April, 1993, the participation of my client was very serious, and therefore they say in paragraph 862, and I quote: "Concerning the conviction on the persecution count, Vladimir Santic's role was most serious since he was a commander who assisted in the strategic planning of the whole attack. He also passed on orders from his superiors to his subordinates which amounted to the reissuing of the orders that were illegal in the circumstances. This role renders particularly grave his participation in the offences committed. Furthermore, he played an active role in the killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians in Ahmici, the destruction of Bosnian Muslim homes and property, and the expulsion of Bosnian Muslims from the Ahmici/Santici region. In particular, Vladimir Santic participated in the attack on the Puscul house, during which the house was burned down, Muzafer Puscul was killed, and the family was expelled from their home after having been forced to witness the murder of Muzafer Puscul. The attack was launched in the early hours of the morning, allowing the victims no opportunity whatsoever to escape." End of quotation. As this important part of the judgement shows, the Trial Chamber assessed that he played a very important role and therefore passed such a severe sentence. Your Honours, there is no doubt that everything I -- that everything I read, everything contained in paragraph 862 merits a severe sentence, of course, if these facts were proven according to standards that were already adopted at this Tribunal, that is to say, that they were proven beyond reasonable doubt. When I previously spoke about the true role of my client in these events, I showed you that the evidence is not conducive to the conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber, and I shall present arguments with respect to each and every one of these matters that will further corroborate this. There is no doubt that the gravity of the crimes does merit severe punishment as this Tribunal has already decided on various occasions, and when that was so, nobody could object. However, my client did not play such a serious role in these events, and this sentence is not correspondent to his role, and I already spoke of Witness AT's statement. Once again, I wish to highlight a few points. The true role of the accused in these events was shown by Witness AT because apart from his testimony, we have no other evidence. Witness EE did not speak about this in a way which would -- actually, when we go back to her statement, we will see that she speaks of the murder of her husband in a different way and that is recognised by the Chamber as well. I would now like to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the very fact that his presence was confirmed in front of the house of Witness EE supports the assertion that that is not the place where a commander could be. The judgement also asserts that Vladimir Santic took part in the strategic planning of the entire attack, and that that is one of the circumstances that makes his role a serious one. There is not a single witness to prove that. There is not a single document that would be conducive to such a conclusion. I quoted the judgement here, the Kordic judgement, that is, and it can be seen where the strategic planning actually took place. Witness Dzambasovic who testified in this case before the Trial Chamber said that even if it were true that the accused was company commander on that level, no strategic planning takes place, just as the judgement said, and this is taken as an important aggravating circumstance. The judgement, furthermore, states - and this was also taken as an aggravating circumstance - that the accused took part in the killing of Bosnian Muslims, the destruction of houses, property; and the Trial Chamber, in the view of the Defence, uncritically espoused these positions as expounded in the judgement. There is no doubt that had the Prosecution had proof of the participation of the accused in the killing of Bosnian Muslim civilians and the destruction of their houses, they would have acted accordingly. Therefore, when the Prosecutor did not charge the accused with any other specific crimes except for that which is alleged in the case of the Puscul family, that means that there was no evidence in this respect, and that would make this part of the judgement invalid. Of course, if this is not valid, then this has to affect the sentence imposed. This is a very serious circumstance and it has special significance. Another circumstance that is taken as an aggravating circumstance in the case of this accused is the following assertion: It is stated in the judgement specifically that the accused took part in the attack on the Puscul house; that it was burned down then and that that was when Muzafer Puscul was killed. If we were to accept that Witness EE's statement is completely true, if we were to accept that everything she said was accurate, then this assertion would be wrong, because this same witness says that she did not see the murder of her husband. She saw that Muzafer was taken behind the shed, and after that she heard shots. So there are no grounds for the judgement in this section, not even in the testimony of Witness EE. If we were to look at all of this, the Defence is convinced that the Trial Chamber made a mistake in evaluating all these facts. There is no doubt that the statement of Witness AT shed light on this role, and I repeat: Had the Trial Chamber been familiar with this statement before, it would have undoubtedly led to the imposition of an adequate sentence. Just another thing. I should like to draw your attention, Your Honours, also to the circumstances which existed which the Defence had set out to prove; however, there is absolutely no trace of them in the judgement. We don't know whether they were given any evaluation, if any, and they should have been evaluated, under Rule 85, according to which any information which would be helpful to the Trial Chamber in deciding on a sentence has to be taken into consideration. Thus, no account has been taken. There was a witness before this Court, a Muslim named Kablar, who availed himself, as he said, of that opportunity to thank the accused Santic, to thank him for his attitude. And they had met for several days. I think that circumstance should have been taken into account in sentencing, which I don't believe the Trial Chamber did. Another thing that failed to be taken into account was the earlier conduct of the accused before all the relevant events. The Defence presented evidence such as D14/6, from which it transpires clearly that the accused had no criminal record, had never been convicted of anything, and his behaviour was exemplary; there is evidence of that. Also not taken into account were the statements of Muharem Pripoljac and a person named Cengic, Muslims who spoke about Santic as a very decent man, devoid of any prejudice, be it religious or ethnic; a person with great ethnic tolerance, a person who frequently helped them. There are also Exhibits D16 and D20 who present the accused Santic in the time before the relevant events in the same light. The Trial Chamber heard witnesses Brkovic and Kocaj as well. All these things which we believe to be very relevant had not been given any weight at all. Another circumstance which was prominent in many judgements made by this Tribunal is the conduct in detention, and we believe it to be relevant in the case of our defendant as well. His behaviour is exemplary. He observes all the rules of the Detention Unit and conscientiously fulfils his obligations, such as they are. He also continues to care for and support his family even from detention. It is also no secret that the accused is ill. Another circumstance which Your Honours have insight into and which deserves to be properly evaluated is that the act was committed reluctantly. I think that in speaking of this it is very important to stress one fact: As my learned friend Mr. Clegg said, this trial would not be taking place for his defendant and for mine as well were it not for one witness, Witness EE. I must ask you to allow me to go into private session for just a couple of sentences, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honours, it has come to our turn after a long wait. My colleagues, Ms. Norul Rashid and Mr. Fabricio Guariglia will deal with two matters, two or three matters. utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Rashid, we're happy to hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, at this stage of the Prosecution's response, I will be addressing the Court on the standard of review that is applicable at the stage of the additional evidence. The Prosecution will forward response to the submissions made by counsel for Drago Josipovic on behalf of the rest of the counsel. The Prosecution will also address the Court on what it thinks is the appropriate standard to be applied. I propose to structure my arguments as follows, Your Honour: I will first of all highlight very briefly the contentious and the nondisputed areas between the Prosecution and the appellants, and then I will highlight the approach that has been adopted by the Appeals Chamber so far in applying the test to be adopted at the hearing stage. The Prosecution would then make certain submissions on what we think is the appropriate standard or the test to be applied by the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal and I will, in the course of my submissions, very briefly reply to some of the appellant's arguments that they have raised as well. Your Honour, with regard to the remedy that the appellants are seeking in relation to this additional evidence, let us be clear as to exactly what they're asking. They want a new trial; they want a rehearing of all the issues and all the evidence that has been adduced at trial on the basis that they have these few pieces of additional evidence. The issue that we have to resolve at this appeal proceeding is what is the test to be applied by the Appeals Chamber in this Tribunal when deciding whether to set aside convictions and order a new trial on the basis of additional evidence. With regard to the contentious areas, Your Honour, we note that they are -- to the nondisputed areas, both parties agree that there are two stages in the determination of the impact of additional evidence: the admissibility stage, where you have the test under 115(A) and 115(B), and then you have the standard to be applied at the hearing stage. What we both are in agreement with is that the standards applicable at both stages are different. What is apparently in contention are that in determining weight at the hearing stage, the appellants argue that the Appeals Chamber is not in a position to consider issues of credibility. They have also advocated for a lower standard; they've asked Your Honour to use the word "might" or "could." And because of these reasons, they argue that inevitably or invariably the Appeals Chamber must always remit the case back to the Trial Chamber because you're not in a position to resolve conflicts of facts or opinion. The Prosecution does not accept that this is the correct or appropriate position for the Appeals Chamber in this Tribunal to adopt, and I will explain why. Counsel has mentioned that the Appeals Chamber has used the word "would" and "could" interchangeably and submits the fact that your previous decisions are of little assistance to what -- to the test to be applied at the hearing stage. What is important to note is that these decisions that have been rendered by the Appeals Chamber were rendered at the admissibility stage. The Appeals Chamber has, in fact, laid down the test for the hearing stage. I will just read from two of your decisions, dated the 26th of February, 2001 and a decision dated the 11th of April this year. This is what you said: "The additional evidence is admitted without prejudice to a determination of the weight to be afforded to the proposed evidence. The Appeals Chamber is correct to conclude that the only issue left to be determined at this stage of the appellate proceedings is weight." So the real mystery here is not the definition of "would," "could," or "might," but what is weight. It would appear from the Appeals Chamber decision that the concept of weight involves an assessment of the credibility which we believe involves assessing the nature, the character, and the probative value of the additional evidence. But this is still not the standard or the ultimate test, Your Honour. This approach of the Appeals Chamber is reflected in all your previous orders made in relation to the additional evidence that has been admitted so far for the purposes of this appeal. I would just highlight a few of the additional -- pieces of additional evidence that have been admitted. Your Honour will recall the admission of the additional statement of Witness CA. This is the crucial distinction which is consistent with the approach that the Prosecution will be proposing today and which might explain why, in certain jurisdictions, the test that several -- some courts have preferred to use is "might" or "could" as opposed to a higher threshold of "would." I will reiterate again that what the appellants is asking the Chamber to do is to quash the conviction. This, I submit, is an extreme remedy. It's reflective of a verdict which is so erroneous that it causes a miscarriage of justice, and a verdict that no reasonable trier of fact would arrive at if the additional evidence was available before it. Still in this light, the evidence offered fort Appeals Chamber's consideration must be of such quality, it has to possess that character that it must have an impact on the verdict. It must be so cogent that if believed, it is likely to produce a different result. In the case of the appellants, an acquittal. The Appeals Chamber appears to have adopted this two-stage test and at the hearing stage those two component test of assessing the credibility and the impact the additional evidence would have on the verdict. If the Prosecution is mistaken in the sense that all issues of credibility has been resolved already by the Appeals Chamber at the admissibility stage, in our submission -- it is our submission that the test that the Court should adopt at this stage is as follows: If the evidence was available at trial and, if believed, whether it would have an impact on the final verdict. The central issue in dispute between the Prosecution and the appellants is in the use and the meanings of the words "could" and "would." What is agreed, Your Honour, is that the difference lies in the higher or lower standard to be adopted. The appellants' rationale for adopting a lower standard is that firstly, the higher standard would inevitably cause injustice as the appellant is never able to meet the standard. He then relies on certain cases, but he acknowledges that some jurisdiction uses the higher standard. The appellants have made no attempts to explain why there is that distinction in certain jurisdiction. The Prosecution submits that the more appropriate test is "would" mainly because it is more responsive to the practice and the nature of the trials conducted at the Tribunal. It is in the interest of justice that this test be adopted because the matter is now before an appellate court. This is not a trial de novo. And lastly, there is ample support for the standard even in domestic jurisdiction. Your Honour, the word "would" does not reflect a sense of inevitability as my learned colleague had submitted. The words "could" and "would," in fact, reflect a degree of likelihood. The Appeals Chamber, I respectfully submit, need look no further than this book for the definition of the word. The word "would" expressed probability and is dependant on the condition to be fulfilled. Your Honour may only look at this book, the dictionary. It denotes a degree of likelihood not inevitability and, in fact, this was the interpretation given by the courts in the US and in Australia as well. The word could means, "able to or to be potentially capable of." The word might expresses, "a possibility based on a condition yet to be fulfilled." Therefore, to give it the meaning proposed by counsel is, with due respect, Your Honour, not of much assistance in appreciating the differing nuances that was conveyed in this context. The appellants argue that the word "would" create a potential for injustice and he has offered an illustration in his brief which he has highlighted in his submissions. The appellant's illustration would not cause injustice because in the illustration that he gives, if someone else admitted to committing a murder and this person was never identified at trial, and if the evidence is sufficiently plausible, a return is warranted unless the Court holds an evidentiary hearing and find that the person is inherently incredible or not worthy of belief. This was, in fact, the situation in the High Court case in Gallagher where someone else admitted to being the murderer in the case but his evidence was rejected because he was not credible and the motion for a new trial was dismissed. Next at paragraph 2.17 of the appellant's reply brief, he argued that the word "could" is consistent with the Appeals Chamber's observation in Tadic that, "Two reasonable person can reasonably come to two different conclusions when presented with the same facts." With respect, this is a misapplication of the principle. The principle refers to the discretion of trial judges and how they are entitled to view the evidence at the trial stage. It was said in the context of the standard of review under Article 25. As to whether or not another court of law or another trial chamber may come to a different or similar conclusion is not a relevant consideration under Rule 115. He next referred to authorities, particularly English authorities, which he says supports his contention. Your Honour, the Prosecution does not deny that various jurisdictions apply and adopt different standards. What the Prosecution will highlight and attempt to rationalise from these cases is the following: What did some courts adopt while others reject the lower standards? What was some of the reasons that they have forwarded? In the English cases that counsel has made submissions on, we assume that counsel is, of course, correct when he asserts that the law in England is clear, and the language used is "might." It would appear that the House of Lords decision that he has referred to is suggestive of this. But Your Honour, the use of the word "might" have to be placed in the proper context, because all the English cases that they have cited deal with jury trials. In a jury trial, there are no written judgements on the factual findings. In fact, the word "might" was only used in these cases where the court decided that they were not sure, one way or another, how the jury may be influenced by the additional evidence. In McNamee, for example, one of the cases cited by counsel, the court laid down the tests as follows, Your Honour, "The only ground of appeal is that the conviction is unsafe because there are three witnesses not called at trial, his testimony is capable of belief and if believed, would or might exonerate the appellant." In this case, the court decided to return the case because it could not be sure how the jury would interpret the evidence. The Court in R and McNamee at registry page 5699 made the same observations: "Accordingly we cannot be sure that a jury on the totality of the evidence which we have heard would have found that they were sure that it was the appellant's fingerprint. This is a matter of importance when we come to the conclusion whether or not the verdict is safe." In Stafford, Your Honour, the Court mentioned three categories -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I will slow down now -- in the case of R. and McNamee, Your Honour, the Court referred to the House of Lords decision in Stafford, and the court mentioned three categories that Lord Cross mentioned in the case of Stafford. utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will try to deal very briefly with the standard of review for sentence and the submissions advanced by my learned friend Mr. Clegg on behalf of all appellants. There are three issues before you on this particular topic. The first one deals with the standard of review for sentence and, in particular, with the impact on the recent Jelisic judgement of the Appeals Chamber on this particular issue. The second issue before you is the one of fresh evidence pertaining to mitigation in its regime on appeal, what is the provision of earning its admission if there is such a provision. The third one would be what is the value of new facts, that is, facts that arise after judgement within the context of an appeal against sentence. As to the first issue, I think that there is only partial disagreement between the parties, and then again that disagreement may be caused due to a misunderstanding on our part of the appellants' position. The second issue is clearly in dispute. And on the third issue, I think that we could say that there is an agreement to the consequence although it may be that the parties reached the same conclusion but through different avenues. I will deal first with the standard of review and the impact of the Jelisic judgement on it. There is clearly no dispute that the appropriate standard for appellate review of sentences is the existence of a discernible error by the Trial Chamber in the sentencing process which has been defined by the Celebici Appeals Chamber in its judgement as a case where an appellant shows to the Trial Chamber either took into account what it ought not to have, or failed to take into account what it ought to have taken into account with the sentencing procedure. The appellants appear to submit that the Jelisic judgement of this Appeals Chamber has varied, a little bit, the standard, and that a sentence may be considered to be excessive if it is not of reasonable proportion with a line of sentences passed in similar circumstances for the same offences. And the appellants further argue that at this stage, there is sufficient jurisprudence in the Tribunal to discern a range of sentences or tariff. The appellants appear to submit that Jelisic would provide a different avenue for a successful review of sentence, one that would be open if an appellant is able to demonstrate that, considering all relevant factors, the sentence imposed is disproportionate in relation to the International Tribunal for the same offences. We respectfully submit that that is not exactly what the Appeals Chamber said in Jelisic, and our position is that Jelisic provides no new avenue but is only a test intimately linked with a discernible error test. To be begin with, the Appeals Chamber stated that, "Whether the practice of the Tribunal is far enough advanced to disclose a pattern is not clear." This is paragraph 96 of the decision. And it added that, "Where there is a significant disparity, the Appeals Chamber may infer that there was disregard of the standard criteria by which sentence should be assessed as prescribed in the Statute and the Rules," and further warned that, "there are a number of factors to be considered in each case." This means that the Jelisic test does not provide an independent avenue for review, but simply a relevant indicator that may enable the Appeals Chamber to conclude that a Trial Chamber committed a discernible error provided that an appellant is able to demonstrate that the cases in question are identical and that the circumstances of which case did not justify a departure from a line of sentences passed for similar offences. So the immediate consequence is that contrary to what would appear to be the position of the appellants, an appellant would not meet the requirement simply by showing the disparity of sentences. Now, the second issue before you is the admission of fresh evidence pertaining to sentence on appeal. And here, the question before you is are where the appellants are entitled to rely for the purposes of an appeal against sentence on evidence that was not before the Trial Chamber and, in particular, whether they could do so, they could rely on that evidence without having to satisfy the strictest for admissibility under Rule 115. As Your Honours may recall, the appellants' position is that -- appears to be twofold. One the one hand since the Trial Chamber is under an duty, unfettered duty under Article 24 of the Statute to consider all the relevant material for the purposes of sentencing, then that duty applies even despite the absolute inactivity from Defence counsel during the sentencing stage. So if it is demonstrated through new material that there was a factor relevant for sentencing that was not considered even due to silence of counsel, then the Appeals Chamber should rely on that new material without the appellant having to satisfy the requirements of Rule 115. The Prosecution opposes this position. And at the outset, it is our submission that this notion of an unfettered duty of a Trial Chamber to analyse all relevant sentencing material even despite a party's absolute inactivity during trial is misplaced in the light of a coherent reading of the Statute, the Rules, and the Tribunal's relevant jurisprudence. Rule 85(A)(vi) clearly establishes that, "It is for the parties to present before a Trial Chamber any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence if the accused is found guilty." This precludes an appellant, as a general principle, from raising for the first time on appeal matters are pertaining to sentence that should have been raised and could have been raised at trial. And this has been clearly repeated in the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal and most recently in the Celebici judgement, the appeal process of the International Tribunal is not designed for the purpose of allowing parties to remedy their own failings or oversights during trial or sentencing. This is Celebici judgement at paragraph 724. Which means that the duty of a Trial Chamber correctly construed under Article 24 is to adequately consider the material placed before it by the parties and not to engage in an accusatorial exercise of incorporating relevant sentencing material which is a task for which we will respectfully add a Trial Chamber of International Tribunal is simply not equipped. And this is, indeed, a consequence of the adversarial character of ICTY proceedings on which counsel for the appellants appear to be relying for other purposes. This means that if an appellant wishes to rely on sentencing evidence that was not adduced before the Trial Chamber, there is no other avenue available than the one provided for in Rule 115. The fact that sentencing material may be a slightly different animal than evidence that goes to establish the guilt or innocence of an accused may have some consequence or may be relevant only to the extent that it may be that that evidence is subject to a different regime for admissibility at trial as the Appeals Chamber appears to have suggested again in the Celebici judgement at paragraph 787. But it's immaterial for the purposes of that material on appeal, and this transpires with clarity from the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber itself in the Jelisic case. When faced with the belated filing of a report on the general practice of the courts of the former Yugoslavia, the Appeals Chamber clearly stated that, generally speaking, for additional evidence to be admitted at the appeals stage, a motion pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules must be presented thereby confirming the applicability to Rule 115 to sentencing material adduced by the parties on appeal. This appears in the judgement paragraph 21. And Your Honours, in the current proceedings when seized with a motion for additional evidence related to sentence adduced by the appellant Zoran Kupreskic, dismissed the said motion on the basis of the criteria for admissibility enshrined in Rule 115 had already been met. I'm referring to the 28 June 2001 decision on motion by Zoran Kupreskic for additional evidence. So there can be no doubt that additional evidence related to sentence is governed, indeed, by Rule 115, and that the -- I would further add that any risk of fundamental unfairness, as has been described by my learned friend, would be averted by the miscarriage of justice exception, which is the natural safeguard to make sure that a technical use of the Rule will not lead to a material misjustice, and which, by the way, would probably take care of the case that Your Honour Judge Wald was putting earlier to my colleague Ms. Rashid. The third issue, and this is the last issue before you as far as the standard of review for sentence is concerned, deals with the value of new facts in an appeal against sentence. The question before you, as correctly identified by my learned friend, is as follows: When new facts and not new evidence have arisen after an appellant's conviction and sentence, what is the value, if any, of these new facts on an appeal against sentence? Guidance may be provided by -- again, by a decision delivered in the Jelisic case by the Appeals Chamber, when a report of post-conviction good behaviour by the appellant was rejected by the Appeals Chamber in the following terms: "The material in question could neither be relevant to any issue before the Trial Chamber nor capable of being considered by it and therefore cannot show that the Trial Chamber committed any error in the exercise of its discretion." I'm quoting the 15 November 2000 decision on the request to admit additional evidence. Accordingly, it would appear that, as a general principle, material pertaining to new facts, to the extent that they are incapable of indicating any error by the Trial Chamber and therefore of rendering the sentence unsafe, are, as a principle, irrelevant and not admissible on appeal. Now, an exception to this principle seems to be the one provided by Rule 101(B)(ii) - that means substantial cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor - which establishes clearly that substantial cooperation post-conviction may be considered in mitigation. Now, presumably the rationale behind this particular exception was to encourage substantial cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor even after a conviction. Now, the interesting thing with this provision is that it clearly had a very high practical value in the days in which the Tribunal had a bifurcated process for conviction and sentencing. The problem that we have now is that that bifurcated procedure doesn't exist any more, and as a consequence, conviction in the current scheme of proceedings before the International Tribunal ordinarily also includes sentence. Therefore, the practical value of the Rule has been or could appear to be significantly limited. So it is our submission that the Appeals Chamber should favour an interpretation of the Rule that ensures its useful effect, and accordingly should entertain cases in which, post-judgement, if we can call it that way, substantial cooperation is raised for the first time on appeal. The Appeals Chamber may choose one of two different avenues before it for this particular exercise. One is to use Rule 101 directly and treat the matter qua an error of law under Article 25(1) and, if it deems that it is in a position to do so, enter a new sentence, if it considers that this should be the appropriate solution for the case. The other avenue would be to treat the matter as a case of review raised in the course of appellate proceedings with exactly the same effect, applying Rules 119 and 122. It is our submission that the Appeals Chamber would have the authority, or it could be sustained that the Appeals Chamber would have the authority for this latter exercise, and we're relying on a separate opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen in the ICTR case, the Prosecutor versus Barayagwiza. "The Appeals Chamber may itself," according to Judge Shahabuddeen, "determine the effect of a new fact in an appeal pending before it." This is the 31 March 2000 decision on the Prosecutor's request for reconsideration, at paragraph 56. This concludes my submissions on standard of review, Your Honour. I was trying to be very brief and only put before Your Honours which are the main points on this particular topic. Needless to say, I'm available to any questions, if there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Questions? One brief one. In the case of substantial cooperation which is raised after the original conviction, is it your position that the Appellate Chamber should decide whether or not whatever has been done amounts to substantial cooperation, or is this something that should be remanded for the Trial Chamber to -- and if so, how does the Appellate Chamber find out if it really was substantial cooperation? Does it have to rely on the Prosecutor saying yes, it was, or does it have to make its own inquiry into what, indeed, the cooperation consisted of? What does the Prosecution think are the mechanics of taking that into consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: I think the answer to Your Honour's question would be that the Appeals Chamber has the discretion in determining in each case whether it has been provided with sufficient material in order to enable the Appeals Chamber to make such a determination, including submissions by the Prosecution as to how the Prosecution considers that cooperation by an appellant to be; whether the Prosecutor, for instance, concedes that the cooperation may amount to substantial cooperation in the sense of Rule 101. And if this is coupled with other materials, such as indicating the precise nature of the cooperation, its impact, for instance, on ICTY proceedings, in other cases, whether this has been relied on by any other Trial Chamber, then the Appeals Chamber may find itself in a position to determine that -- to determine two questions: First one, whether the cooperation amounts to substantial cooperation under Rule 101(B); and if the answer to that question is yes, whether that should be reflected on sentence. And if the Appeal Chamber feels that it is not fully equipped to deal with that, it clearly has the option to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me put it to you, Mr. Guarigilia: Is the Prosecution, in this case, telling the Appeals Chamber that there has been substantial cooperation in the case of -- in the case that we know about, or is it saying, well, maybe you want to look into it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: The position of the Prosecution, well, has been, I think, quite clear. We considered that the cooperation amounts to substantial cooperation under Rule 101. We acknowledge at the same time that the determination on whether that is the case or not is a judicial determination. So we can assist the Appeals Chamber, but clearly it is the Appeals Chamber's determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me go one step further. Do you think you've already given us by way of your submissions, written and otherwise, enough material for us to make the determination now, or would we, in your view, have to make a separate inquiry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: I was going to deal with that topic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, that's all right. As long as you deal with it at some point, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: I will deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I will now give the floor to Ms. Rashid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will now utilise the time available from now up till 5.15, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify that. I said 5.15, you were right, originally, but then we took our break earlier. I would say till about five after five now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll work within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this part of the Prosecution response, I will be addressing the Chamber on the submissions made by my learned colleague Mr. Clegg on the evidence of Witness EE. Your Honour, the Prosecution has made substantive submissions in its response brief and I can do no better than to refer Your Honour to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. response brief. I would, however, for purposes of this appeal, highlight certain factors, certain facts which I am of the view that the Appeals Chamber should look at when evaluating the Trial Chamber's decision in relation to Witness EE. Your Honour, before I proceed to discuss the evidence of Witness EE, may I just highlight two fundamental principles which I have elaborated in the Prosecution response brief. The first relates to what we call the extension of the test of materiality. The emphasis there is that even if discrepancies found within a witness's evidence are material and pertain to certain aspects of the witness's evidence, the Court is entitled to reject those aspects of the witness's evidence, but that does not lead to an automatic rejection of the witness's entire evidence or other aspects of the witness's evidence which the Court believes. This proposition finds support in the Trial Chamber's decision in Celebici, which I have highlighted in my response brief, and I have also -- what I have done is to highlight cases from various domestic and civil law jurisdictions, Your Honour, from the United States, from Asia, Australia, and the UK, which supports this proposition. The second fundamental principle that I would refer to is the one made by the Trial Chamber in Celebici and in the ICTR decision of Rutaganda. The Trial Chambers in these cases observe that under the circumstances where pre-trial statements are being tendered to discredit or impeach the credit of a witness, under the circumstances, the Trial Chamber attaches probative value to testimony primarily on the basis of oral testimony given in the courtroom as opposed to prior statements, where the demeanor of the relevant witnesses could be observed firsthand by the Trial Chamber and placed in the context of all the other evidence before it. This is because the Court acknowledges that there are -- there are certain circumstances that the Trial Chamber must look at when looking at the prior inconsistent statements of witnesses; for example, the sitting time lapse between the events about which the witnesses are testifying; the making of the prior statements and their testimony before the Trial Chamber; the difficulties that witnesses may experience in recollecting precise details years after the fact; and the near impossibility of being able to recount them in exactly the same detail and manner on every occasion that one is asked to do so. It is against these principles that I would ask Your Honours to cast your minds when you evaluate or review the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to Witness EE. It is interesting for the Prosecution to note that counsel for Drago Josipovic has stayed clear of Witness EE's evidence in court, but what he has done is that he has reiterated arguments offered at the trial relating to the inconsistencies in Witness EE's statement and her mistaken identification of two soldiers. All these arguments were considered by the Trial Chamber and rejected. One thing that has to be borne in mind is that the Court can only rely on evidence adduced under oath to support its factual findings. Investigative statements are not evidence. They have been used here in this case solely for the purpose of impeachment. What we cannot get too distracted from the evidence that has to be studied. Counsel has barely addressed the Court on her evidence in court. Evidence which the Trial Chamber has obviously relied on. The reason is simply they, they could not seriously fault her evidence in court. I will deal with all the challenges that counsel has made to Witness EE's statement, but what I would like to bring your attention to is what we believe are the fundamental features of Witness EE's evidence which clearly influenced the Trial Chamber to accept her evidence and -- not in it's entirety but in certain pertinent and material aspects. We have mentioned in our response brief about the chain of consistency relating to her identification of Drago Josipovic as one of the perpetrators that committed the acts on 16 of April in the Muzafer Puscul house. The Trial Chamber found that Witness EE's testimony and identification of Drago Josipovic were, in fact, strengthened by her previous investigative statements which demonstrate this chain of consistency. The statements show that in all her previous statements to various investigators, various persons, as well as in court, Witness EE consistently named the appellant Drago Josipovic as one of the soldiers that had appeared at her doorstep on the morning of 16th of April, 1993. She had never wavered from that evidence. The Trial Chamber also heard evidence that Witness EE knew the appellant since childhood. He was a close neighbour. She said that she would see him frequently while travelling to and from work and while visiting neighbours. In her statements and in court, not only did Witness EE speak of the appellant being one of the soldiers at her doorstep on the morning of 16th of April, she was also consistent on specific details about his conduct thereafter, and his conduct during the attack itself. In view of her consistent identification of the appellant, it was open to the Trial Chamber to conclude that her identification of the appellant at the scene at the material time was accurate and reliable. A proper evaluation of Witness EE's evidence is not to truncate her evidence at the time of the attack as to what she saw and what she could not possibly have seen, that is, she must have made a mistake since she possibly made a mistake in identifying two of the soldiers, then she must have made a mistake in identifying the rest. We have to look at her evidence in its totality. Witness EE spoke about seeing the appellant Drago Josipovic on two occasions. Once in the morning during the attack, and subsequently in the evening later at the barn where he was hiding. Drago Josipovic and another person called Livancic came and asked her to leave the shed. Now, counsel for the appellant has made no mention of the events occurring after the attack. We cannot view her evidence in isolation of all the other events that she spoke about because it is improbable that the witness could have made a mistake on the appellant's presence during the attack but was not -- but did not make a mistake subsequently in the evening when she saw him at the barn. The witness also spoke of certain details which the -- involving the appellant. She said that it was the appellant who came to the shed that day. He broke the lock. He let the farm animals out at her request. The appellant also agreed to accompany her to Anto Papic's house to seek shelter. This was after the attack on the same day in the evening because she said she was afraid to walk out on her own. It must be noted, Your Honour, this aspect of the witness' evidence was not disputed. In fact, it was supported by [redacted] himself who was called by the Defence. With regard to the appellant's assertion that she has -- she had misidentified the soldiers on various occasions, that, with all due respect, is exaggeration, is an exaggeration. It is submitted at that time to the Trial Chamber was probably correct to counsel conclude that she may have been mistaken only in relation to with respect to two of them. In fact the Trial Chamber said "may" because the Trial Chamber had correctly given the benefit of the doubt to the appellant. The Prosecution notes that the Trial Chamber also accepted that the witness was not mistaken about the presence of another person, Livancic, and they gave reasons for concluding this. That's at paragraph 503 of the judgement. In fact, Your Honour, Witness EE has consistently named Livancic as one of the perpetrators. Lastly, Your Honour, it is imperative to place Witness EE's evidence in its proper perspective. Her evidence was material to establish the charges against Drago Josipovic and Vladimir Santic. The Prosecution notes that the bulk of the inconsistencies highlighted by the appellant pertain to other soldiers and their movements and their conducts. The presence of the rest of the soldiers, their identities, their exact movements are not relevant for the purpose of deciding whether there was sufficient evidence to prove that the appellant Drago Josipovic was present at the scene and committed the crimes he was convicted for. They are relevant in so far and only to the extent of determining her voracity, Witness EE's voracity. The probative value, Your Honour, of these inconsistencies must be placed in their proper perspective, and it has to be placed tangential to the fundamental features of Witness EE's evidence, her consistent and unwavering identification of the appellant, and her consistent narration of his conduct during the attack and subsequent to the attack. The appellants, Your Honour, they want this Court to accept a strange and improbable theory of what had happened, that the witness was either mistaken, she had either fabricated evidence that occurred in the morning, but she was perfectly credible and accurate on events in the evening where the appellant had performed certain acts of kindness in agreeing to save her farm animals and walking her to Anto Papic's house. How could she have been mistaken about all these details? Why would she want to fabricate evidence in -- relating to the attack, but not subsequently? How was it that she had made a mistake about the appellant's presence during the attack but not subsequently? Therefore, the witness' evidence cannot be seen in terms of isolated events. It has to be seen as a whole. Her account, her story flows from the time of the attack until the time she was made to leave Ahmici and she told the Court, very clearly, the appellant's role from morning to evening. If you look at her evidence in it's entirety pertaining to Drago Josipovic, there are no gaps. There are no inconsistencies. Your Honour, it is also clear from the judgement that the Trial Chamber was perfectly aware of the problems in hearing this witness' evidence. They were perfectly aware that she had given inconsistent statements which we do not deny that she had. The Trial Chamber considered at length and evaluated the evidence that was adduced to discredit her. After considering all this evidence, they decided to accept the fundamental features of her evidence they were entitled to. They were best placed to hear and assess the witness' evidence, and they have given very clear reasons as to why they believed her. The appellant, Your Honour, has not established that the Trial Chamber erred in fact or in law on relying on Witness EE for its factual finding. We respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to Witness EE's evidence do not warrant review by the Appeals Chamber. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Rashid. Well, it's a bit under time, it's five after 5.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you complete are your submission in time. We will adjourn in just a second. I have only one question for Mr. Yapa. Mr. Yapa, are you in a position vis-a-vis Mr. Abell's motion here to the President for disclosure of certain portions for the Prosecution's closing brief, are you in a position to tell us whether or not the Prosecution is going to oppose that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: We will not be opposing the motion as such. I think the question earlier was whether we were in a position to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, there are questions, you're right. If you are in a position to admit or concede, that would, of course, alleviate a lot but if not, I at least wanted to know in terms of pursuing this whether you opposed to the motion. There are two questions. One may alleviate the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: In the first position we could say we will not opposing the motion, but we are not in a position to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right I have your position. With that, we will let the Prosecution complete their case tomorrow morning. We start at 9.00 and hopefully finish before 5.00 tomorrow. Thank you. I do want to thank the translators for the extra time that they've spent all day. I know it's been an onerous day, and we're much in their debt. Thank you.
